prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "SPACE EXPLORATION TECHNOLOGIES CORP" (ticker SPCX), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "SPCX", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Space Exploration Technologies Corp.
result.industry: Space launch, satellite broadband and AI
markets: Orbital launch services (Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, Starship)
Human spaceflight and government space (Dragon, NASA, US national security)
AI models and compute (xAI Grok, Colossus data centers)

mission.statement: Our mission is to build the systems and technologies necessary to make life multiplanetary, to understand the true nature of the universe, and to extend the light of consciousness to the stars.
mission.source: SpaceX Form S-1 registration statement (May 2026), Prospectus Summary, 'Our Mission'
mission.plain: SpaceX wants to help people live on other planets, understand the universe and spread life and intelligence into space.

about.plain: SpaceX builds rockets that can land and fly again, which made getting to space much cheaper. It uses those rockets to put up thousands of Starlink satellites that beam fast internet to homes, ships, planes and phones almost anywhere on Earth. It also flies astronauts to the space station for NASA. Since 2026 it also owns xAI, which makes the Grok chatbot and the X social network, and rents out giant AI computers.
about.customers: Millions of households and businesses buying Starlink, airlines and shipping firms, NASA and the US military, satellite companies needing launches, and AI companies such as Anthropic renting computing power.
about.everyday: Starlink dishes bring internet to rural homes, cruise ships and airline Wi-Fi, and Grok is the chatbot inside X (formerly Twitter).

money.plain: Satellite internet subscriptions and dishes for homes, ships, planes and governments
Falcon rocket launches, Dragon astronaut flights and NASA/defense contracts
Grok AI, X advertising and subscriptions, and renting AI computers
Direct-to-cell satellite service for ordinary mobile phones
Giant fully reusable rocket for Moon/Mars trips and AI computers in orbit

result.summary: SpaceX has one of the widest moats in industry: reusable Falcon rockets give it the lowest cost to orbit (it carried over 80% of the world's mass to orbit in 2025), and that cheap launch lets it run the only large-scale satellite broadband network, Starlink, with over 10 million subscribers. The AI segment (xAI/X) is a newer, loss-making bet where its advantage is far less clear.

pricingPower.evidence: In launch SpaceX has raised Falcon 9 list prices since 2022 while still winning most commercial missions; in Starlink it chose volume over price, with average revenue per user falling from $99/month (2023) to $66 (Q1 2026) as subscribers grew from 2.3M to 10.3M and Connectivity revenue rose 50% in 2025.

moats.evidence: SpaceX and Starlink are globally known brands linked with Elon Musk, and it holds valuable spectrum rights (including spectrum bought from EchoStar in 2025) and NASA crew certification.
Starlink users own dishes tied to the network and governments/airlines sign multi-year contracts, but consumers could switch to fiber or Amazon's satellite service where available.
More Starlink subscribers fund more satellites, which improve speed and coverage and attract more users; X and Grok have classic social network data effects.
Over 85% of missions fly on reused boosters and SpaceX launched about 170 times in 2025, giving it a cost per kilogram rivals cannot match and letting it deploy 9,600+ Starlink satellites cheaply.
Low-orbit broadband needs thousands of satellites and huge launch capacity, so only a few players (SpaceX, Amazon, Chinese state networks) can exist, and SpaceX has years of head start.
Rival rocket makers like ULA and Arianespace built businesses on expensive expendable rockets and cost-plus contracts, so copying rapid reusability would undercut their own models.

Vertical integration (in-house engines, avionics, satellites, user terminals) and rapid iterate-and-test engineering, shown by about 650 Falcon launches with a 99%+ success rate, are extremely hard to copy.
Elon Musk's leadership and SpaceX's ability to attract top aerospace engineers, plus scarce orbital slots and spectrum licences already secured, are hard for rivals to obtain.

customers.evidence: Starlink subscribers grew from 4.4M (2024) to 8.9M (2025) and 10.3M (March 2026) across about 164 countries, and airlines such as United and Qatar Airways adopted Starlink Wi-Fi; NASA relies on Dragon as the main US crew vehicle, though Grok and X face more mixed user sentiment.

talent.evidence: SpaceX is consistently one of the most sought-after employers for engineering students in surveys such as Universum's, attracting top aerospace talent despite a reputation for very long hours and demanding management.

product.evidence: Falcon 9 is the world's most-flown, most reliable rocket (over 650 launches, 99%+ success) and Starlink is the leading satellite internet service in speed and coverage; Starship, the largest rocket ever flown, had completed 11 test flights by mid-2026 but has yet to reach orbit operationally.

competitors.note: Claude competes with Grok, though Anthropic is also a major customer renting Colossus compute

marketShare.measure: mass to orbit (SpaceX S-1: 'more than 80%' in 2025)

threats: Amazon's Kuiper/Leo constellation and Chinese state networks (Qianfan, Guowang) could cut Starlink's pricing and share; Starlink ARPU already fell from $99 to $66 per month
Starship delays or failures would hold back next-generation Starlink V3 satellites, Moon/Mars plans and orbital data centers
The AI segment lost $6.4B at the operating level in 2025 and AI capex hit $15.8B in Q2 2026 alone; xAI may not earn a return against OpenAI, Google and Anthropic
The Anthropic compute contract (~$1.25B/month) can be terminated on 90 days' notice
Key-person and governance risk: Elon Musk holds about 85% of voting power and divides time across Tesla and other ventures
Dependence on US government (about one-fifth of 2025 revenue) and political/regulatory risk, including foreign landing rights and spectrum rules
Legal and regulatory probes around Grok and X (copyright, explicit imagery, data protection)
Space debris, collision and orbital-congestion rules could limit constellation growth

ceo.name: Elon Musk
ceo.background: Founder, CEO and CTO; University of Pennsylvania degrees in physics and economics (Wharton); co-founded Zip2 and PayPal, CEO of Tesla

c1.evidence: SpaceX leads the fast-growing commercial space economy, carrying over 80% of global mass to orbit in 2025 and running the largest satellite internet network (10.3M Starlink subscribers by March 2026).

c2.evidence: Customers choose SpaceX because reusable Falcon rockets are cheaper, more frequent and more reliable than any alternative, and Starlink offers fast internet anywhere; this lead in reusability and vertical integration has lasted a decade and rivals are still years behind.

c3.evidence: SpaceX and Starlink are household names and the default leaders in rockets and satellite internet, much as Tesla is for EVs, and Starlink users widely recommend it in rural areas.

c4.evidence: Since 2002 SpaceX has repeated its mission to make life multiplanetary, and Musk's pay package is tied to a self-sustaining Mars colony of one million people; ten years of this would transform space access.

c6.evidence: “innovative, rockets, Elon Musk, Starlink” — the impression is mostly positive and admiring, though polarized by views of Musk and his politics.

c7.evidence: SpaceX's S-1 claims a total addressable market above $28 trillion (space $370B, broadband $1.6T, AI services $26.5T), riding secular trends in global connectivity, space and AI.

c8.evidence: Direct-to-cell mobile service, in-flight and maritime connectivity, AI compute, orbital data centers, Moon landers for NASA's Artemis and Mars missions give it many large new markets.

m1.evidence: Musk founded SpaceX in 2002 with the explicit goal of making humanity multiplanetary and pursued reusable rockets when the industry said it was impossible.

m2.evidence: Musk is the founder, CEO and CTO, has led SpaceX for 24 years, famously sleeps at factories during crunches and nearly put his last money into SpaceX in 2008.

m4.evidence: Musk is customer-obsessed about cost and capability, but he is known as a very demanding boss rather than a servant leader, with frequent reports of harsh treatment and long hours.

m5.evidence: He built a culture of rapid iteration, 'test, fail, fix' and first-principles engineering that produced Falcon 9 reuse, Dragon, Starlink and Starship.

m6.evidence: As chief engineer/CTO Musk is directly involved in rocket and Starship design decisions despite having a physics rather than a formal engineering degree.

m7.evidence: His goal of making humanity multiplanetary is bigger than profit, but his public conduct, politics and treatment of staff are highly controversial.

m7b.evidence: Elon Musk gave the Caltech commencement address in 2012 and spoke at USC Marshall School of Business commencement in 2014.

m8b.evidence: Musk is one of the most distinctive and recognizable business personalities in the world, known for bold goals and a heavy social media presence on X.

m9.evidence: SpaceX went from three failed Falcon 1 launches to about 170 launches in 2025, built Starlink to 10M+ subscribers and $11.4B of 2025 revenue, and restored US crew launch capability in 2020.

m10.evidence: SpaceX is famous for cost-cutting through vertical integration and using off-the-shelf parts, slashing launch costs versus traditional aerospace contractors.

c10.evidence: Starlink brings internet to over 10M customers in about 164 countries, including remote villages, ships, disaster zones and Ukraine, and cheaper launches enable weather, science and GPS satellites worldwide.

p2.evidence: Landing and reflying orbital rockets and running a 9,600-satellite constellation are among the hardest engineering feats ever achieved, and they matter for national security, science and global connectivity.

f1.evidence: Recast revenue grew from $10.39B (2023) to $14.02B (2024) and $18.67B (2025), and H1 2026 was up 54%, but audited figures before 2023 were never published.

f2.evidence: Gross margin improved from about 41% (2023) to about 49% (2025), but operating margin swung from loss to a small 2024 profit and back to a 14% loss in 2025 as AI spending soared.

f3.evidence: After the IPO SpaceX held about $100.0B of cash and marketable securities against $39.4B of debt and finance leases at June 30, 2026, with $127.2B of shareholders' equity, though capex far exceeds operating cash flow.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow reached about $6.8B in 2025, but operating income has been volatile (a $2.6B operating loss in 2025 versus a $466M profit in 2024) because of xAI and Starship spending.

v1.evidence: Falcon 9 is clearly the best rocket for most customers (cheapest per kilogram, most flights, reused boosters) and Starlink is the only fast internet in many rural or remote places.

v2.evidence: SpaceX ranks among the most desired employers for engineering students in Universum-style surveys thanks to its mission, but Glassdoor-type reviews highlight long hours and burnout, so it rarely tops 'best place to work' lists.

c5.evidence: If SpaceX disappeared, NASA would lose its main way to fly astronauts and cargo to the ISS, the US military and satellite firms would lose most launch capacity, and millions of rural, maritime and airline Starlink users would lose internet.
